Form IV + نا subject + ه object; 'We sent it down'

drop the ه object pronoun
the نا is the root

prompt: For بِسَلَامٍ, why is a host-only gloss 'peace' unsafe, and what are the display classes?

concept: the dual ending is licensed only by a referent of exactly two
prompt: For الْمُعَلِّمَانِ, what does the ending -ani require about the referent, and what must you check before applying a dual ending to any noun?
expected_answer: The ending -ani marks the dual and is licensed only when the referent is exactly two (here, two teachers); before choosing a dual exponent you must count the referent, because the same shape is not available for 'more than two' or for a generic plural sense.
accepted_variants: -ani marks dual, licensed only for a referent of exactly two; count first
the dual ending requires exactly two referents, checked before the ending is applied
forbidden_answers: the dual ending can mark any plural referent
-ani is just a stylistic variant of the plural
the number of the referent does not matter for choosing the ending
required_reasoning: licensing condition checked before the exponent is chosen

concept: dual and sound-plural oblique endings share a letter; number is read from the vowel before it
prompt: In the oblique (non-nominative) forms, the dual ending -ayni and the masculine sound-plural ending -iina both end in nun. If a learner names the correct number (dual or plural) but points only to the final nun as proof, is that answer trustworthy? State which parts of the ending must be read, in order, to tell them apart.
expected_answer: No -- the shared final nun is not enough on its own to tell dual from plural, because dual -ayni and plural -iina both end in it; the discriminating evidence is the vowel before it: a fatha plus ya marks the dual, a kasra plus ya marks the sound masculine plural. Naming the right number while pointing only at the shared nun is right for the wrong reason.
accepted_variants: reading only the final nun cannot separate dual from plural; check the vowel before it -- fatha+ya marks dual, kasra+ya marks the sound plural
the shared nun is not diagnostic; the discriminating evidence is the vowel that precedes it in the ending
forbidden_answers: the final nun alone tells you it is dual
the final nun alone tells you it is a sound plural
dual and sound-plural oblique endings cannot be told apart
required_reasoning: shared final nun named as not enough on its own

concept: the suffixal (sound) masculine plural is licensed only for rational referents
prompt: Can مُهَنْدِسُونَ (engineers) and an attempted كِتَابُونَ (for 'books') both use the suffixal -uuna plural? What must be checked before attaching -uuna to a noun?
expected_answer: مُهَنْدِسُونَ is licensed because its referent (engineers) is rational (human); كِتَابُونَ is not a real Arabic plural because a book is not a rational referent, so كتاب takes a different (broken) plural instead. The rationality of the referent must be checked BEFORE the suffixal masculine plural -uuna/-iina is attached -- the ending is not available just because the noun is masculine.
accepted_variants: the sound masculine plural -uuna requires a rational (human) referent; check rationality first, not just gender
muhandisuuna is licensed by a human referent; a non-rational noun like kitaab cannot take -uuna and needs a broken plural
forbidden_answers: any masculine noun can take the suffixal -uuna plural
kitaabuuna is a correct plural of kitaab
rationality of the referent does not matter for choosing the plural
required_reasoning: rational referent identified for the licensed example
non-rational referent identified for the rejected example
licence checked before the plural ending is attached

concept: the mafaul (passive-participle) template applies only to Form I; settle the verb form first
prompt: Is مَكْتُوب the passive participle of a Form-I verb or of an augmented form? What must you check before assuming a word follows the mafaul template?
expected_answer: مَكْتُوب is the Form-I passive participle of كَتَبَ (he wrote), following the bare-triliteral mafaul template. That template belongs only to the unaugmented (Form I) class; an augmented verb (Form II mufaal, Form IV mufal, and so on) uses a different passive-participle shape. You must settle which form class the verb belongs to before assuming any word instantiates the mafaul template.
accepted_variants: mafaul is the Form-I passive-participle template only; augmented forms use a different shape, so check the form class first
settle Form I vs augmented before applying the bare-triliteral patient template
forbidden_answers: every passive participle in Arabic follows the mafaul template
the form class of the verb does not matter for the participle's shape
augmented forms also use mafaul
required_reasoning: mafaul identified as the Form-I-only template
form class checked before the template is applied

concept: a hollow (weak-middle) root does not take the canonical mafaul skeleton unchanged
prompt: Root ق و ل is hollow (its middle radical is weak). Does its passive participle keep the plain mafuul skeleton, like مَكْتُوب does for ك ت ب? What must be classified first?
expected_answer: No -- a hollow root like ق و ل does not carry the canonical mafuul skeleton unchanged; the weak middle radical forces a different surface shape (maquul, not a form matching mafuul letter-for-letter). Before instantiating any participle template you must classify whether the root has a weak position (hollow, assimilated, or defective), because a weak radical changes the template's surface, not just its meaning.
accepted_variants: hollow roots do not take the plain mafuul skeleton unchanged; classify the weak radical first
a weak middle radical reshapes the participle template; check for a hollow root before applying mafuul as-is
forbidden_answers: every root takes the same mafuul skeleton regardless of weak letters
hollow roots are identical to sound roots for participle formation
the weak radical can be ignored when building the participle
required_reasoning: hollow root recognized as a weak-middle-radical class
canonical mafuul skeleton rejected for this class
weak position classified before the template is instantiated

concept: the mim-prefixed place/time noun's vowel is keyed to the present stem, not the past
prompt: For the place-noun of جَلَسَ (he sat), present-tense يَجْلِسُ, is the mim-prefixed noun مَجْلَس or مَجْلِس? What stem must you check to decide the vowel?
expected_answer: It is مَجْلِس, with a kasra after the lam, because the present stem يَجْلِسُ has a kasra on the second radical; the mim-prefixed place/time noun's vowel is keyed to the PRESENT stem's vowel, which the past-tense stem جَلَسَ does not reveal on its own. Checking only the past form cannot settle the prefix vowel.
accepted_variants: majlis takes its vowel from the present stem yajlisu, not from the past jalasa alone
the mim-noun's vowel is decided by the present-tense stem vowel; the past stem is not enough
forbidden_answers: the past-tense stem alone decides the mim-noun's vowel
majlas and majlis are interchangeable spellings of the same word
the mim-prefixed noun's vowel is fixed and never varies by verb
required_reasoning: present stem consulted for the vowel
past stem rejected as sufficient on its own
correct vowel attached to the mim prefix
